sections.heading: Converting between polar and rectangular coordinates

questions.q: Convert the polar point $\left(4,\dfrac{2\pi}{3}\right)$ to rectangular coordinates.
Convert the rectangular point $(-3,3)$ to polar coordinates with $r>0$ and $0\leq\theta<2\pi$.
questions.answer: $r=\sqrt{(-3)^2+3^2}=\sqrt{18}=3\sqrt{2}$. Since $(-3,3)$ is in Quadrant II, $\theta=\pi-\dfrac{\pi}{4}=\dfrac{3\pi}{4}$. Polar point: $\left(3\sqrt{2},\dfrac{3\pi}{4}\right)$.

sections.heading: Converting polar equations to rectangular form

questions.q: Convert the polar equation $r=4\cos\theta$ to rectangular form, and identify the curve.
questions.answer: Multiply both sides by $r$: $r^2=4r\cos\theta$, so $x^2+y^2=4x$. Completing the square: $(x-2)^2+y^2=4$ — a circle of radius $2$ centered at $(2,0)$.

questions.q: Convert the rectangular equation $x^2+y^2=9$ to polar form.
questions.answer: Since $r^2=x^2+y^2$, the equation becomes $r^2=9$, so $r=3$ — a circle of radius 3 centered at the pole.

sections.heading: Visualizing a rectangular ($r$ vs. $\theta$) graph of a polar rose

questions.q: The graph shows $r=3\cos(2\theta)$ plotted in rectangular form, with $\theta$ on the horizontal axis (in radians) and $r$ on the vertical axis — a standard technique for analyzing a polar rose curve before sketching it.
parts: State how many petals the actual polar rose $r=3\cos(2\theta)$ has, using the rule for $r=a\cos(n\theta)$ with even $n$.
Read off the graph: at which values of $\theta$ in $[0,2\pi)$ does $r=0$ (these are the angles where the rose curve passes through the pole)?
answers: When $n$ is even, the rose $r=a\cos(n\theta)$ has $2n$ petals; here $n=2$ gives $4$ petals.

$r=0$ when $\cos(2\theta)=0$, i.e. $2\theta=\dfrac{\pi}{2},\dfrac{3\pi}{2},\dfrac{5\pi}{2},\dfrac{7\pi}{2}$, so $\theta=\dfrac{\pi}{4},\dfrac{3\pi}{4},\dfrac{5\pi}{4},\dfrac{7\pi}{4}$ — matching the four zero-crossings shown.

questions.q: Identify the type of curve represented by $r=2+2\sin\theta$ and state its key feature.
questions.answer: This is a cardioid (heart-shaped curve), since it has the form $r=a+a\sin\theta$ (or $\cos\theta$) with equal constant and coefficient. It passes through the pole when $\sin\theta=-1$, i.e. $\theta=\dfrac{3\pi}{2}$.

questions.q: Determine whether the graph of $r=3\cos\theta$ is symmetric about the polar axis (the $x$-axis), and justify your answer.
questions.answer: Replacing $\theta$ with $-\theta$: $r=3\cos(-\theta)=3\cos\theta$, unchanged. So the graph is symmetric about the polar axis.

sections.heading: Multiple representations of the same polar point

questions.q: Give two other polar representations of the point $\left(5,\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right)$: one with a negative $r$-value, and one with a different positive angle (adding $2\pi$).

A radar station models the range of its signal by the polar curve $r=6+2\cos\theta$ (in km), where $\theta$ is measured from due east. Find the maximum and minimum detection range, and the direction of each.
questions.answer: Maximum range: $r=6+2(1)=8$ km, at $\theta=0$ (due east). Minimum range: $r=6+2(-1)=4$ km, at $\theta=\pi$ (due west).

sections.heading: Distance between points in polar form

questions.q: Find the distance between the polar points $\left(3,\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right)$ and $\left(5,\dfrac{2\pi}{3}\right)$ by first converting both to rectangular coordinates.
Classify each polar equation as a circle, cardioid, limaçon (with inner loop), or rose, and briefly justify: (a) $r=5$, (b) $r=2+4\sin\theta$, (c) $r=4\sin(3\theta)$.
questions.answer: (a) $r=5$ is a circle of radius 5 centered at the pole (constant $r$). (b) $r=2+4\sin\theta$ has $|a|<|b|$ (here $a=2<b=4$), so it is a limaçon with an inner loop. (c) $r=4\sin(3\theta)$ has the rose form $r=a\sin(n\theta)$ with odd $n=3$, giving a 3-petaled rose.

sections.heading: Points of intersection of polar curves

questions.q: Find the values of $\theta$ in $[0,2\pi)$ where the polar curves $r=2$ and $r=4\cos\theta$ intersect.

Explain, without evaluating an integral, why the polar area formula $A=\dfrac{1}{2}\int_a^b r^2\,d\theta$ uses $r^2$ rather than $r$, by comparing it to the area of a circular sector $A=\dfrac{1}{2}r^2\theta$.
questions.answer: A circular sector of radius $r$ and angle $\theta$ has area $\dfrac{1}{2}r^2\theta$ — note the $r^2$, since area scales with the square of the radius. The polar area formula generalizes this by summing infinitely many thin sectors, each with area $\dfrac{1}{2}r^2\,d\theta$, which is exactly why $r$ (not $r^2$ or $r^{1}$ alone without justification) appears squared in the integrand.

questions.q: A circular sector has radius $6$ and central angle $\dfrac{\pi}{3}$. Use the sector-area formula $A=\dfrac{1}{2}r^2\theta$ to find its area.
